--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page begins the preface of Abraham Hinckelmann’s 1694 edition of the Quran, the first complete Arabic text printed in Europe. The catchword "for" (nam) indicates the start of his defense against potential critics.</meta>

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER

->Sends Fondest Greetings<-

## ABRAHAM HINCKELMANN, DOCTOR

When I first applied my mind to publishing the Arabic text of the Quran, I easily foresaw that I would run into the censures of many men—especially those who are idle and unskilled. From these, I have chosen three primary objections to dissolve in this preface, as they seemed to do no small amount of work in increasing the envy toward my undertaking. The first of these is: *That the use of both the Quran and of Arabic studies as a whole is quite meager; that good hours and the labors of human genius could be better spent than on these trifles and nuances, from which, in the end, you carry away little besides the vain praise of knowledge, if not of ostentation.* To this is added a second: *If any work was to be placed in this book, it should have been expected from someone other than a Theologian; certainly, in a Pastor of Hamburg (as someone has written publicly), such an undertaking is deservedly disapproved.* To these a third is added, perhaps full of meager malice: *That this work could have come forth far more splendidly and polished if the proper care had not been lacking; that it should have been enriched with a Translation, a Commentary, a Refutation, and other ornaments, so that it might please an age so delicate.* To these accusations, I shall reply not with everything that could be said, but with what seems necessary to me—

<summary>Abraham Hinckelmann introduces his 1694 Arabic edition of the Quran by addressing three major criticisms: the perceived uselessness of Arabic studies, the impropriety of a Christian pastor editing an Islamic text, and the lack of a translation or commentary in this specific volume.</summary>
<keywords>Abraham Hinckelmann, Quran, Arabic studies, Hamburg, theology, 17th-century printing, Islamic studies in Europe</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the author's defense of his scholarly method, specifically the necessity of documenting heretical beliefs to better refute them. Catchword "ve-" likely leads into "veritas" or "venerabilis" on the following page.</meta>

To Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose anti-heretical writings served as a model for later theologians</note>, and to so many other writers, both ancient and modern alike, it seemed most advisable and in the best interest of the Church to review the profane and—for the most part—utterly futile doctrines of the heretics themselves, using their own words and writings as much as possible. By doing so, suitable material might finally be supplied to pious minds for either despising or refuting those errors. I have judged that I must do the same regarding this most pestilential plague of the East <note>original: "Orientis lue"; likely referring to Islam or Eastern Christian schisms from a Western perspective</note>, so that at long last, that entire system might be laid bare and exposed to our people. Thus, under favorable auspices, certain exceptional minds might be called upon for the solid extinction of this monster.

If there are those who judge that this work should be received with insults and mockery, let them enjoy the intemperance of their own nature as far as I am concerned; I, indeed, shall never repent of this plan, however much it may vex them. And who, I ask, would repent of contributing through some labor—such as this modest effort of ours—to the common good, which may one day do much to illustrate the glory of Christian doctrine? For its truth, not in the least hindered by the madness and futility of its enemies, always scatters brighter rays the more it is attacked by that darkness. For although the loss of so many souls surpasses all other calamities and all the sorrows of mortals, nevertheless, from this very discord, a greater heavenly [truth...]

<summary>The author defends his decision to publish the "futile" doctrines of Eastern adversaries, arguing that exposing error in its own words is the most effective way for the Church to refute it and highlight Christian truth.</summary>
<keywords>Augustine, heresy, Eastern plague, polemics, Christian doctrine, refutation, defense of scholarship</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>The text continues the author's justification for his scholarly work, following the catchword "gu-" from the previous page.</meta>

For if I had believed that I was undertaking a useless labor, or merely shaking a sterile oak tree <note>A Latin idiom meaning to engage in fruitless work</note>; surely I was not born with such an absurd disposition that I would not have withdrawn my hands as soon as possible. But truly, a completely different reasoning for this entire matter has become clear to me. 

For as far as the **Quran** <note>original: "CORANUM"</note> is concerned, although it contributes so little to the salvation of those who bestow their faith upon it that it becomes instead the cause and occasion of eternal destruction; and although it adds little or nothing to other sciences beneficial to the human race through its own doctrine: there is nevertheless something else which can rightly be judged not unworthy of the Christian office, glorious to the Church, and conducive to the salvation of infinite souls, if divine grace (of which we must not despair) grants its favor. 

For since no heresy can be opposed with the proper weapons, nor can the wretched mortals held captive by them be extricated from the snares of cunning, unless its true face, its limbs, and the structure of its whole body (or rather, its corpse) be thoroughly known to us: we shall allow ourselves to be led into the hope of conquering **Mohammedanism** <note>original: "Muhammedismi"; a historical term for Islam</note> in vain, unless we hear the **Impostor** <note>The author refers to Muhammad from a 17th-century polemical Christian perspective</note> himself pouring forth his sacrilegious oracles in that very language in which he presented them. Indeed, there is no certainty in a translation <note>original: "versio"</note>, nor is a sufficient judgment possible from fragments scattered here and there. Therefore, what was necessary for **Epiphanius** <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his writings against heresies</note>, the Author...

<summary>The author argues that studying the Quran in its original language is essential for the Church to effectively refute Islamic doctrine and convert its followers. He contends that one cannot defeat a "heresy" without thoroughly understanding its internal structure and original texts.</summary>
<keywords>Quran, Islam, Christian apologetics, linguistics, translation, Epiphanius, religious polemics, Arabic studies</keywords>

# Preface

...they will notice that the origin of this Prophecy is dull, and that everything in the entire book is heaped together without order or connection—what else? without mind—full of so many contradictions, so many stale fables of the Jews and Pseudo-Christians, so many tiresome and almost innumerable repetitions, so many insane lies fighting against the very Nature of things, and so many proofs of the incestuous life of its own Prophet. In a word: they will see it is filled with a heavy hand with everything that could, above all others, suit and distinguish a Fanatic, an epileptic, an <term>Idiot</term><note>In this 17th-century context, "Idiot" refers to someone unlearned or lacking formal education, rather than a modern slur.</note>, an Impostor, and a shameful man among all the Corruptors of every age. For no one even slightly skilled in these matters will deny that everything in the affairs and doctrine of Muhammad is arranged in this way. 

There came forth a Man born to Idolatrous Parents, and instructed in that same impiety which he followed until the fortieth year of his age; he was void of all wisdom and learning, except what he could learn from his own people, the <term>Quraysh</term><note>original: "Koreischitis"; the ruling tribal group of Mecca to which Muhammad belonged.</note>, while devoted to the <term>mule-driver's art</term><note>original: "Mulioniæ arti"; a reference to his early career in the caravan trade.</note> from his 16th to his 25th year. He calls himself so many times in the <term>Quran</term><note>original: "Corano"</note> the <term>Unlettered Prophet</term><note>original: "نبي الأمي" (Nabi al-Ummi); the author translates this as "Prophetam Idiotam" to emphasize a lack of education.</note>, and was even charged with a lack of humanity by that Oracle of his in <term>Surah Al-Imran</term><note>Chapter 3 of the Quran.</note>, verse 153: *Even if you are harsh and hard-hearted, yet they will not separate themselves from you.* <note>original: "ولو كنت فظا غليظ القلب"</note> This man, seized by the epileptic disease—which is familiar to Fanatical temperaments—

<summary>This page presents a polemical critique of Muhammad's character and the Quran, characterizing the text as disorganized and the Prophet as an unlearned, "epileptic" impostor. It reflects the harsh, confrontational style of early modern European scholarship regarding Islam.</summary>
<keywords>Muhammad, Quran, Quraysh, epilepsy, polemic, Surah Al-Imran, Prophet, education</keywords>

the more support truth received, the more strongly and easily it repressed those struggling against it. The <term>charlatans</term><note>original: "Agyrtæ," referring to wandering quacks or religious impostors</note> of so many centuries bear witness to this themselves; in order to fascinate as many minds as possible, they labored with all their zeal to conceal their true feelings and their more destructive dogmas, being conscious of their own powerlessness. And indeed, it is not to be doubted that if our ancestors had lent their ears to the <term>Council of Vienne</term><note>A church council held in 1311-1312 which, among other things, proposed the establishment of chairs for Hebrew, Arabic, and Chaldean languages to aid in missionary work.</note> and had vigorously cultivated <term>Arabic studies</term>, which have grown old in the meager late-night labors of so few Cardinals and Monks, a brilliant victory over Muhammadan impiety might have been hoped for. Many weapons against the infidels could have been supplied, and noble minds could have been trained for so holy a war. Care for these matters must now be undertaken as if by <term>right of recovery</term><note>original: "postliminio," a legal term for the restoration of rights to someone returning from captivity.</note>; it may be troublesome at the start, but it will one day wonderfully commend itself by its very result. It would be a long delay and involve many twists and turns if I were to set forth the entire history of a religion propagated through so many frauds and slaughters.

The number of Christian authors can scarcely be counted. 

Here, we are chiefly looking at the Quran itself, regarding whose *authors and fate* we shall still offer some warnings. Those who attribute the entire work to Muhammad are wonderfully mistaken. <sig>d</sig>

<margin>Possessed by the Devil.</margin>
Having been snatched away, after he had frequently shut himself in caves and tormented himself with fasts even to the point of madness, he began to persuade first himself, and afterwards others—especially his wife Khadija—that he was hearing divine discourses. For he presented to her, in the first instance, those words as if received from the Angel Gabriel, which now finally appear in the 96th chapter: *Read* (from this, the name Quran <note>original: "قرأن"</note> is believed to have been derived, unless it was rather designated by a Jew so that it would correspond to the ancient Miqra <note>original: "מקרא" - a Hebrew term for the Hebrew Bible, meaning 'that which is read'</note>) *in the name of your Lord, who created man from clotted blood: read by your Lord, who taught man what he previously did not know.* The wife, being wiser than her husband, tended to mock the new Prophet and seriously warn him about the deceptions of the Devil. To this pertains the complaint in the 15th Sura <term>Sura: a chapter of the Quran</term>, verse 7: *And they say, "O you to whom the book* (the Quran) *is sent,"* <note>original: "انك مجنون"</note> *"surely you are insane,"* or rather (for this is the force of the word, from whose root the word <gloss>Jinn</gloss> denotes a Demon, from which the Italian *ingannare* <note>to deceive</note> and the Norwegians' *Gan* <note>sorcery/magic</note> have their origins) <insert>possessed by a spirit.</insert> He, having become more embittered by the woman's warnings—as is the way with such temperaments—and at the same time so that he might more easily conceal his illness, ordered himself to be covered with mats and linens. From this, there still appear Chapter 73, whose inscription is the Sura <note>original: "المزمل"</note> *The Enwrapped One*, and Chapter 74, the Sura <note>original: "المدثر"</note> *The Shrouded One*. See Jalaluddin <note>original: "Gelaloddinus" - likely referring to the famous commentator Jalaluddin al-Mahalli or al-Suyuti</note> in his commentary on both...

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly critique of the Quran's sources, specifically focusing on the origins of Islamic narratives in Christian and Persian traditions.</meta>

*Hottinger* <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667), a Swiss philologist and theologian</note> pursues this in book 1, chapter 3 of his *Oriental History*, page 150 and following. From where else was the entire eighteenth chapter of the Quran, titled *The Cave* <note>Surah Al-Kahf</note>, born, along with the little story of the Seven Sleepers? This was taken from a spurious tradition among the ancient Christians concerning the seven youths of Ephesus who hid themselves in a cave during a time of persecution. See the complete treatise on these men by *Gregory of Tours* <note>A 6th-century bishop and historian</note> in Volume 11 of the *Great Library of the Fathers*, page 959; also *Eutychius* in the *Alexandrian Annals*, page 391 of the Pococke edition; likewise *Gregory Abul-Pharaj* <note>Bar Hebraeus, a 13th-century scholar</note> in *Dynasty VII*, page 128; *Sheikh Saadi* in the *Persian Rose Garden*, book 1, chapter 6 of *Olearius's* German edition (for it is missing in the Persian original); also in *Gentius's* Persian-Latin edition, page 55. See also Ibn Idris in the *Geography*, commonly called the *Nubian* <note>The work of al-Idrisi</note>, near the end of the fifth climate, fourth part, pages 275 and 276 of the Latin edition. *Baronius* <note>Cesare Baronio, a Catholic historian</note> mentions this in the *Roman Martyrology*, page 506, where he himself laughs at these trifles, just as they do not appear in the older *Martyrology* published at Lucca and commonly attributed to *Jerome*. See *Florentini's* notes on that work, page 746. And why say more? You will rarely find any chapter here in which plagiarisms from Christian books—both the sound and the blameworthy—do not occur. I shall add only one more. There was circulating at that time a well-known little book about the miracles of the Christ Child, commonly under the title of the Gospel written by Peter. The full title is: The Book <note>original: "کتاب" (Kitab)</note>

<summary>The author argues that the Quranic story of the Seven Sleepers is plagiarized from Christian legends and cites numerous historical and geographical sources to prove the narrative's derivative nature. He concludes that Islamic scripture frequently borrows from both canonical and apocryphal Christian texts.</summary>

<keywords>Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, Surah Al-Kahf, plagiarism, Hottinger, Gregory of Tours, Sheikh Saadi, apocryphal gospels, Islamic origins, Christian tradition</keywords>

...others are plainly excluded. For he had much interaction with men of both religions <note>referring to Judaism and Christianity</note> in Syria, where Muhammad practiced trade for a time. Regarding the two servants in the workshop of a sword-smith in Mecca, who themselves read the Pentateuch <note>the first five books of the Old Testament</note> and the Gospels to him, see the testimony of Al-Zamakhshari <note>a medieval Persian scholar of the Quran</note> in Marracci, Part 1 of the *Introduction*, pages 241 and 242. Many learned men have observed traces of Nestorianism <note>a Christian doctrine emphasizing the separation of Christ's divine and human natures</note> here. But other heresies that arose among Christians also have points in common with his decrees in various places. Thus, what is read in the *Chapter of Imran* <note>Surah Ali 'Imran</note>, verses 79, 82, 83, and 84, clearly tastes of Novatianism <note>a rigorous early Christian sect that refused readmission to those who had lapsed during persecution</note>. There are also places where he disputes against the heretics. The things he proposes in the *Chapter of the Cow* <note>Surah Al-Baqarah</note>, verse 73, graze against the Origenists <note>followers of the early theologian Origen</note> who deny the eternity of the punishments of hell. He could not even restrain himself from occasionally mixing in the very words of the New Testament. Thus, what is read in *Surah* <insert>The Cave</insert> <note>original: "كهف" (Al-Kahf)</note> verse 20: *And do not say of anything, "I will do it tomorrow," unless (you add) "if God wills."* Are these not the very things read in the *Epistle of James*, chapter 4, verses 13 and 15? From the mouth of which mortals, however, did he receive the fables known and believed only by the common and unlearned Christians? Who related to him those things concerning *George the Martyr* <note>Saint George</note>, which in many...

It is observed from the Arabic root *radakha* <note>original: "رضخ"</note> that it means "he struck with a club, a stone, etc."

In the same place, the phrase *sons of Resheph* <note>Hebrew: בני רשף; Job 5:7</note> is commonly translated as *Sons of the coal*, although the root *rashafa* <note>original: "رشف (רשף)"</note> denotes a rapid throwing or the brandishing of a weapon, and refers to a specific manner of hurling. Hence also in Psalm 76:4, we find the *arrows of the bow* <note>Hebrew: רשפי קשת</note>.

In the same chapter, verse 26, our High Interpreter writes again that the word *kelah* <note>Hebrew: כלה; often translated as "full age" or "maturity"</note> **causes trouble for the translators**. But it causes no trouble for the Arabs, for whom that word entirely points to the state and age of a *filicernium* <note>A term for an old man near death, literally one who attends his own funeral feast</note>. For the root *kalaja* <note>original: "كلج"</note> proves this, by which someone is signified as having such a harsh, gloomy, and contracted face that he even shows his teeth.

The noun *taphel* <note>Hebrew: תפל</note> in chapter 6, verse 6, expresses not only food without salt, but in general anything thick, such as legumes, lacking in taste and fragrance. The origin *taphal* <note>original: "دفل"</note> teaches this. Similarly, in the same place, *challamut* <note>Hebrew: חלמות</note> is not the **white of an egg yolk**, but the Arabic *khaluma* <note>original: "خالومة"</note>, meaning **milk froth**, which Hottinger already observed before me in his *Oriental Smegma* <note>A scholarly work by Johann Heinrich Hottinger, 1658</note>, page 152.

In the same chapter, verse 15, the word *bagadu* <note>Hebrew: בגדו</note> by no means signifies **they acted treacherously**, since no one attributes that to a river; rather, the usage in Arabism must be considered, where *bajada* <note>original: "بجد (בגד)"</note> means **it stopped** or **remained**, so that it is either used ironically, or the root itself (as is observed in many other cases) also possessed a contrary meaning. The word *abus* <note>original: "عفت" (afat)</note> means *he bent, twisted, or distorted.* In Chapter VII, verse 6 <note>referring to the Book of Job</note>, the verb *vaimas* <note>original: "וימאס"</note> should be explained according to Arabic usage, where *mas* <note>original: "ماس"</note> signifies: *the wound opened wide.* In this way, it responds well to the preceding word *la'ad* <note>forever</note>. It is used thus in the Arabic translation of Matthew 18:28: "and he seized him <insert>and choked him</insert> <note>original: "وحنقه" (wa-hanaqahu)</note>." Therefore, Job likely referred to a suffocating catarrh <note>an excessive buildup of mucus</note> or a similar kind of disease from which he preferred to die.

In Chapter VIII, verse 16, the interpreters are again stuck on the word *ratub* <note>original: "רטוב"</note>. Among the Arabs, this very word <note>original: "رطب" (ratab)</note> is taken for *moist, fresh, green, soft, or tender.* Compare Luke 23:3. In Chapter IX, verse 9, there is a strange disagreement regarding the stars. Samuel Bochart <note>a famous 17th-century French biblical scholar</note> rightly advised in his *Hierozoicon* (Volume II, Book 1, Chapter 16) that the word *Ayish* <note>original: "עיש"</note> was formed by dropping the first letter from the Arabic *Na'sh* <note>original: "نعش"</note>, and expresses the "bier" or the constellation of the Great Bear <note>Ursa Major</note>. For those stars which the Latins called the *Septentriones* <note>the seven plowing oxen</note>, the Arabs likened to a funeral bier, just as the Greeks likened them to a wagon. They therefore called the quadrangle of both bears the "bier" <note>original: "نعش" (na'sh)</note> from the act of lifting; and the three stars that constitute the tail of both bears they called the *daughters or sons of the bier* <note>original: "بنات نعش" (Banat Na'sh)</note>, who namely precede the bier as is done in funeral processions. # On the Excellence of Arabic Poetry

In the work *On Correct Hellenism* <note>original: "in Ἑλληνισμῷ ὀρθῶς"</note> on page 95, he adds that he believes this with a willing heart, since **Arabic** <term>Arabismus: the Arabic language and its idioms</term> is a most refined, copious, magnificent, and august language: especially as it follows rational rules in its pronunciation. 

But there are many other things which ennoble Arabic Poetry. The greatest part of it is occupied not with profane trifles, but with the praise and illustration of the most excellent matters. Thus, you may hear some singing of the stupendous perfection of the divine Nature, others of the sweetness of divine love, others of the union of our mind with God, and others of the beauty of the virtues. There are those who illustrate the deeds of Emperors and Heroes. Truly, you would lack nothing elegant in **natural Theology** or **moral Philosophy** that the Arabic Poets do not exhibit. 

This art was rooted, as it were, in the very lineage of this nation, and perpetually propagated from the furthest memory. *The erudition of the Arabs,* says **Gregory Abulpharagius** <note>A 13th-century Syriac Christian scholar and historian, also known as Bar Hebraeus</note>, *whose glory had been their chief pursuit, was this:* <gloss>knowledge of their tongue, the rules of their language, the weaving of poems, and the composition of orations</gloss> <note>original Arabic: علم لسانهم واحكام لغتهم ونظم الاشعار وتاليف الخطب</note>. What more? The Arabs even attributed the preservation of their language to Poetry itself. See **Pococke** <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), a famous English Orientalist</note> in his *Specimen*, page 158 and following. Also, no nation has always held Poets in such high honor; none has rewarded even a few verses with such great gifts—

To be blind to this, and to rattle on about useless studies where the highest utility commends itself to everyone—what is that but to be insane with a touch of reason? From Poetry we pass to Oratory. In this art, it cannot be denied that Rome and Athens added far greater refinement, judgment, and especially knowledge of civil affairs than you will find among the Arabs. But when you consider their sharpness of invention, the propriety of their words, their subtlety in thinking, their incredible breadth in varying their style of speaking, and that <term>euphony</term> <note>original: εὐφωνίαν; refers to the pleasing, melodic quality of speech</note> rightly understood by few (which some have fruitlessly mocked in the Arabs under the name of *Asiatic swelling* <note>A derogatory term used by some classical scholars to describe a style they considered overly ornate or "puffy."</note>), their abundance of sentiments, and the gravity of their subject matter, you will find this nation to be in no way inferior, if not superior.

Would that some learned man might one day publish for us the complete work of HARIRI! <note>Al-Hariri of Basra (1054–1122), famous for his 'Maqamat,' a masterpiece of Arabic rhetoric.</note> He is publicly explained as the "Cicero of the Arabs" in all the Academies of the East, and according to the testimony of Golius <note>Jacobus Golius (1596–1667), a celebrated Dutch Orientalist.</note>, he has earned such great praise *that to this very day, hardly any other author is considered more suitable for students in Asia and Africa from whom they may learn the propriety of the Language, and at the same time its abundance and elegance.* We possess a copy written in the East in the clearest script with a continuous Commentary, the abundance and use of which (as well as of other manuscripts) we offer to all those who will bring their learning and zeal to its publication. Besides Hariri, there is still a great crowd of Orators—

Just as Greek and Roman writers were, by a wondrous fate, translated into the Arabic language, many historians experienced the same fate as well. Among these was the incomparable **Livy** <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian whose monumental history of Rome is largely lost to us.</note>, who—would that he might be rescued whole from the shadows of Fez <note>Referring to rumors that complete manuscripts of Livy's lost books existed in the libraries of Fez, Morocco.</note> and brought into the light, even in a rough translation! Indeed, with the same success that *Bernegger* <note>Matthias Bernegger (1582–1640), a scholar known for his work on the historian Quintus Curtius Rufus.</note> restored Curtius, the illustrious **Gronovius** <note>Johann Friedrich Gronovius (1611–1671), a leading classical scholar and editor of Livy.</note> would easily restore Livy to us, and perhaps with even greater skill.

In the field of *Literary History*, how mutilated and defective everything is among our scholars! This is for no other reason than that the true appearance and succession of the doctrines that flourished in the East remain unknown to us. But here, if anywhere, Arabic literature comes to our aid. For by its help, the decrees and hieroglyphics of the Chaldeans, Egyptians, Persians, Syrians, and Indians, as well as the schools of their philosophers and priests—along with infinite other matters pertaining to these subjects—are revealed, both in those times about which the Greek writers are entirely silent, and in later ages. For the Eastern peoples have always shown themselves to be scrupulous in preserving the traditions of their ancestors. I have been permitted, and am still permitted, to contemplate this in a distinguished example: namely, in a manuscript codex with which my collection was enriched by a man of illustrious and magnificent character...

The languages of the Bohemians <note>Czechs</note>, the Poles, and in part the Russians, have not yet entirely shed their Hebrew character. Never, however, have such great expeditions been made by Europeans from these lands into Syria, Arabia, and Persia that they could have carried their own language to those peoples. Furthermore, the *authority of God himself* confirms this, claiming the first cultivation of Europe for Japheth and his descendants (who are surely of Hebrew stock). This is further proven by the Greeks themselves, who everywhere acknowledge *Japetus* <note>The Greek Titan Iapetus, whom the author identifies with the biblical Japheth</note> as the ultimate ancestor of their race.

Although the *colonies of these descendants of Japheth* are shrouded in the darkest night, and little or no help can be expected from the historians who still survive in Europe for an accurate knowledge of the migrations of Eastern peoples into more remote lands—and moreover, those events which occurred in different centuries undoubtedly underwent various and singular transformations—nevertheless, the matter itself, or rather the speech which we carry daily in our mouths, or which we read in the most ancient writings of the European nations, leads us to a most certain conjecture of our first origin, even where the light of History fails.

Whatever the case may be, and though one might rightly despair of attaining a perfectly clear understanding of the *migration of nations through every age*, it nevertheless seems most evident to me that the path by which one reaches the true and original remains of the Germanic and Latin (I add also the Greek) languages **looks toward the East**. For others who wander off in all other directions, their undertaking will prove a deception; they are swept away into trackless wastes and thrust upon us the phantoms of their own imagination as true origins. In this regard, I do not know if the Greek Grammarians might hold the first prize for such folly. But let others, more abundant in leisure and talent, see to that. I shall now set forth the one thing that remains (the *first* in order), producing examples in both languages that will perhaps whet the appetite <note>original: "salivam... motura" - literally "to move the saliva," an idiom for stimulating interest or hunger</note> of more noble minds.

We shall begin with the LATIN language. In this, the word *Alo* <note>to nourish or raise</note> is from the Arabic <term>علا (Ala)</term>, meaning to nourish, feed, or support. This work is uniquely concerned with asserting the splendor and victory of the Christian faith. Those who criticize it have neither rightly estimated all that I have brought forward from the beginning until now regarding the use of the Quran and Arabic studies <note>original: "Arabismi"</note>, nor have they sufficiently noticed what was in the prayers of Luther and other supreme theologians, and what men of the highest dignity in the Church before me judged to be not unbecoming for themselves. For who finds fault with Luther or Schweigger <note>Salomon Schweigger (1551–1622), author of the first German translation of the Quran</note> for a German version of this book? They attempted to refute it, but what did they refute other than imperfect and mangled things communicated by others? etc.* The immortal theologian Wolfgang Franz praises these words in his *Treatise on the Interpretation of Scripture, page 40*, adding shortly thereafter: *I would altogether desire that all boys be applied more maturely to the Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic languages, since everywhere in other schools, and sometimes in some of ours, one notices even bearded young men only then becoming accustomed to those exercises.* From the Reformed side, let Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> also be heard again in his praised letter to Cappel, page 854: *While you seek the Quran, printed even in an elegant character with a translation and notes, you ask for a Chimera <note>A mythical beast; here meaning an impossible or non-existent thing</note>. To undertake its printing...*

Finally, we must approach the *last point of these accusations*, in which a dispute is needlessly raised against us concerning the *Translation and elegance* of the work; we freely admit that the former was omitted by choice, while in the latter, some fault may be ours. Regarding the translation, I confess that many things deterred me. For I will say nothing now of the great disagreement among Interpreters in the more difficult passages (the chief cause of which is a search for order that was sought in vain); nor shall I bring up the difficulty to be overcome in this *Augean stable* <note>A reference to the Greek myth of Hercules cleaning the stables of King Augeas; used here to describe a task that is incredibly filthy, difficult, and neglected.</note>, where almost every corner is filled with trifles and empty repetitions. There were certainly other reasons which, partly by force and partly by design, were able to withdraw me from that labor. Chief among these is that I believed a Translation of the entire book would be a source of deception and harm to *Arabic literature* <note>original: "Arabicæ litteraturæ"</note> rather than of use. No example here is more illustrious than that which the *Greek writings* <note>original: "Græca scripta"</note> rendered for us in *Europe* offer. At one time, several individuals both in *Leiden* <note>original: "Leida," a major center for printing and Oriental studies in the Netherlands</note> and in *England* had desired the printing of this work. However, certain STUBBORN MEN <note>original: "MOROSI HOMINES"</note> among our own circles thwarted the project, though I do not know what reasons moved them. Indeed, this book is capable of seducing no one, seeing as nothing is more dull-witted than its contents. Since it is already published and available in the *Latin, French, and Italian* languages, why could it not also be printed in ARABIC—a language which few are proficient in, and those few are less likely to be led astray by the common folk? Therefore, let my censors allow these defenses; I cannot persuade myself that I could lose my case, unless perhaps in the court of *Envy*. Nor do I deeply repent the labor I have undertaken.

Rather, I praise and acknowledge with a grateful heart the integrity of that man most celebrated for his solid erudition, *Master Tezel* <note>original: "Dn. Tezelii," likely referring to a contemporary scholar or patron</note>. As soon as he had perceived something of our purpose, he publicly declared in his most learned work, the *Ephemerides* <note>A scholarly journal or diary of the period</note>, that he not only favored the project but that this labor was not unworthy of a theologian. I prefer to please minds of that caliber than the entire flock of those who think nothing is right except what they do themselves. Indeed, by the habits and rumors of such men, many extraordinary talents have been crushed, and many branches of knowledge have been undermined as if by tunnels <note>An image of secret sabotage or sapping a fortification</note>, so that the Church and the Christian Commonwealth have suffered irreparable damage. Meanwhile, mastery over good literature and most useful studies is handed over to those for whom an intolerable and publicly harmful audacity takes the place of wisdom.

If all these works published in print up to now had been produced only in the original language, and with just and accurate care applied throughout, so that our scholars approached their reading aided only by Glossaries and other Grammatical supplements, perhaps less would be granted to the ambition of the many; yet, you would certainly find a no less accurate knowledge of <term>Hellenism<note>original: "Græcismi"; refers to the mastery of the Greek language and its nuances</note></term> everywhere. A third copy—more elegant and correct than any we have ever observed—was added to our library by that jewel and immortal glory of theologians, **DR. JOHANNES DIECMANNUS** <note>Johann Diecmann (1647–1720), a prominent German theologian and educator</note>. He is the General Superintendent in the Provinces of Bremen and Verden, illustrious for his merits among all good men; to him we also owe a Persian commentary on the greatest part of the Quran, written purely and with <term>diacritical points</term> <note>original: "punctis"; these are marks added to Arabic script to clarify pronunciation and meaning</note> added throughout. Nor were we lacking other manuscripts, though they were imperfect and less comparable to those we have praised. Finally, the famous commentary of Jalal al-Din <note>Refers to the "Tafsir al-Jalalayn," a classic Sunni interpretation of the Quran</note> brought us great assistance, from which we sought help whenever necessary, and never in vain. And these are generally the sources to whom credit must be given for whatever is laudable in our edition. One remains, whom I would be ungrateful to pass over, because I used his help in such a way that I confess, without him, I might have succumbed to the burden. **SEBASTIANUS** <note>Likely referring to Sebastian Schmidt, a noted Hebraist and theologian</note>

## Chapter of the Pilgrimage <note>Surah Al-Hajj</note>, Meccan
### Seventy-eight Verses

->In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful<-

1. O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the convulsion of the [Final] Hour is a mighty thing. 2. ->**18.** We subjected the mountains to bear witness with him, glorifying God in the evening and at sunrise. **19.** And the birds were gathered together; all were turning to Him in praise. <note>The text describes the miraculous harmony of nature joining David in his psalms of worship.</note> **20.** We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive speech. <note>original: "fasl al-khitab" — referring to the ability to judge clearly and speak with authority.</note> **21.** And has the news of the litigants reached you? When they climbed over the wall into the sanctuary— **22.** When they entered upon David, and he was terrified of them. They said, "Fear not. We are two litigants; one of us has wronged the other, so judge between us with truth and do not be unjust, and guide us to the even path. **23.** Indeed, this is my brother; he has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe; so he said, 'Entrust her to me,' and he overpowered me in speech." **24.** David said, "He has certainly wronged you in demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes. And indeed, many associates oppress one another, except for those who believe and do righteous deeds—and how few they are." And David realized that We had only tried him, so he asked forgiveness of his Lord and fell down bowing and turned in repentance. <note>This passage is traditionally interpreted as a parable sent by God to test David's own conduct and sense of justice.</note> **25.** So We forgave him that; and indeed, for him is a near access to Us and a beautiful place of return. **26.** O David, indeed We have made you a successor <term>Khalifa: a vicegerent or representative of God's authority</term> upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the way of God. Indeed, those who go astray from the way of God will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Account. **27.** And We did not create the heaven and the earth and that between them aimlessly. ...the light; and indeed, God is to you most Kind, most Merciful. * 10. ### CHAPTER SIXTY ###

<margin>10. Section</margin>
> O you who believe! When believing women come to you as emigrants <note>original: *muhājirāt*, referring to those fleeing Mecca for Medina</note>, then examine them. Allah knows best as to their faith. If you find them to be true believers, do not return them to the disbelievers. These women are not lawful for them <note>the disbelieving men</note>, nor are those men lawful for them. Give the disbelievers back what they have spent <note>referring to the bridal-wealth or *mahr* paid by their former husbands</note>. There is no blame on you if you marry them, provided you give them their due compensation <term>mahr: a mandatory gift given by the groom to the bride at the time of marriage</term>. Do not hold onto marriages with disbelieving women. Ask for the return of what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent. This is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise. ۩

<margin>11.</margin>
> And if any of your wives have gone from you to the disbelievers, and you then have your turn <note>referring to gaining spoils or reaching a new treaty</note>, then give those whose wives have gone the equivalent of what they had spent. Fear Allah, in whom you are believers. ۩

<margin>12. Section</margin>
> O Prophet! When believing women come to you to pledge their allegiance, promising that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children, nor bring forth a slander they have fabricated between their arms and legs <note>original: *yaftarīnahu bayna aydīhinna wa-arjulihinna*, an idiom referring to falsely attributing a child to a husband or claiming a foundling as their own</note>, nor disobey you in what is right, then accept their pledge and ask Allah to forgive them. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful. ۩

<margin>13. Section</margin>
> O you who believe! Do not take as allies a people with whom Allah is angry. They have despaired of the Hereafter just as the disbelievers have despaired of the inhabitants of the graves <note>this refers to those who do not believe in the resurrection of the dead</note>. ۩

<summary>This page concludes Surah Al-Mumtahanah, detailing the "Pledge of the Women" and the legal protocols for dealing with female converts migrating between hostile territories. It emphasizes the dissolution of marriage ties between believers and disbelievers while ensuring financial fairness through the reimbursement of dowries.</summary>

<keywords>migration, marriage law, dowry, pledge of allegiance, Al-Mumtahanah, faith examination, Hereafter</keywords>

-> — In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful ❊ — <-

<margin>1. 1.</margin> When the hypocrites <term>hypocrites: those who feigned interest in Islam for political or social gain while secretly opposing it</term> come to you, they say, "We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah." And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are surely liars. ❊
<margin>2. 2.</margin> They have taken their oaths as a cover <note>original: "junnatan," meaning a shield or protection used to hide their true intentions</note>, so they averted others from the way of Allah. Indeed, evil is that which they have been doing. ❊

<margin>4.</margin> And when you see them, their physical forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. <margin>propped up</margin> They are as if they were propped-up pieces of wood <note>a metaphor for being hollow or lifeless despite a sturdy outward appearance</note>. They think every shout is against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded? ❊
<margin>5.</margin> And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads away and you see them evading while they are arrogant. ❊
<margin>6. 6.</margin> It is all the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; never will Allah forgive them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people. ❊
<margin>7.</margin> They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse." And to Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth, but the hypocrites do not understand. ❊
<margin>8. 8.</margin> They say, "If we return to Medina, the more honored will surely expel therefrom the more humble."

<summary>This page concludes the 87th Surah (Al-A'la), emphasizing the continuity of its message with the scriptures of Abraham and Moses, and begins the 88th Surah (Al-Ghashiyah), which vividly contrasts the punishments of the Fire with the rewards of Paradise.</summary>
